sources.entry: A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector: a very insightful guide about Go's GC

summary.title: A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector
summary.one_liner: Learn how Go's mark-sweep tracing garbage collector works, how GOGC and the memory limit trade CPU time against memory, and how to reason about GC costs.
takeaways: Go uses a non-moving, tracing mark-sweep GC that walks the object graph from roots and then sweeps unmarked heap memory.
GC cost model: memory cost is roughly live heap from the previous cycle plus new heap; CPU cost is a fixed per-cycle cost plus a cost proportional to live heap.
GOGC sets the trade-off between GC CPU and memory: doubling GOGC roughly doubles heap overhead and halves GC CPU cost.
The memory limit (GOMEMLIMIT / SetMemoryLimit, Go 1.19+) is a soft cap; the GC limits itself to about 50% CPU to avoid thrashing.
Values that escape to the heap are dynamically allocated and managed by the GC, while non-escaping values use stack allocation.
summary.summary: This guide explains the Go garbage collector for developers who know Go but not GC theory. It defines tracing garbage collection, objects, pointers, roots and the mark-sweep cycle, and contrasts Go's non-moving collector with moving collectors. It then builds a simple cost model for GC CPU and memory using steady-state examples, and explains how GOGC and the Go 1.19 memory limit tune that trade-off. Interactive visualizations on the page illustrate the effects, and it closes with thrashing and advice on using the memory limit.
